ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Located in Guizhou, the “China Sky Eye” is currently the world's largest-aperture single-dish radio telescope (FAST). Through FAST, the viewing angle between Mercury and the Sun is measured as $\theta$ (the angle between the lines connecting Mercury and the Sun respectively with the observer), as shown in the figure. If the sine value of the maximum viewing angle is k, and the motions of Earth and Mercury around the Sun are regarded as uniform circular motion, find Mercury's orbital period.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure there is an observation point labeled FAST, and near the right side is labeled “Sun”; a smaller circular orbit is drawn around the Sun, and “Mercury” is labeled on the orbit. Two sight lines from the FAST observation point respectively to the Sun and Mercury form an included angle θ at the observation point; a larger circular orbit is also drawn on the outside, representing the orbit of Earth/FAST moving around the Sun with Earth. Reasoning: When the viewing angle θ of Mercury relative to the Sun reaches its maximum value, the line of sight from FAST to Mercury is tangent to Mercury's circular orbit around the Sun, so the radius from the Sun to Mercury is perpendicular to the line of sight from FAST to Mercury. Let the radius of Earth's orbit around the Sun be R, and the radius of Mercury's orbit around the Sun be r. Then in the right triangle formed by FAST, the Sun, and Mercury, the angle θ is at FAST, the Sun—Mercury distance r is the opposite side of this angle, and the FAST—Sun distance R is the hypotenuse, so sin θ_max = r/R. The problem gives sin θ_max = k, therefore r/R = k. From Kepler's third law T_M^2/T_E^2 = r^3/R^3, and Earth's orbital period T_E = 1 year, obtain T_M = (r/R)^{3/2} years = k^{3/2} years = sqrt(k^3) years. Final answer: sqrt(k^3) years.
